title: DNS Resolution Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on how DNS resolves names: recursive vs iterative lookups, the root/TLD/authoritative hierarchy, core record types, TTL and caching, and the dig/nslookup tools.

chapters.title: DNS Mental Model
points: DNS maps names to data (mostly IPs) through a distributed, hierarchical database; read a name right to left: www.example.com. = root . → com → example → www
Stub resolver (your OS) asks a recursive resolver (ISP, 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) which does the work; authoritative servers hold the real answer for a zone
Three server tiers: root servers (13 named identities a–m, many anycast instances) know the TLD servers; TLD servers (.com, .org) know the domain's NS; authoritative servers hold the records
A zone is the portion of the namespace one set of authoritative servers manages; a delegation (NS record) hands a subtree to another zone
DNS uses UDP/53 by default and falls back to TCP/53 for large responses (truncated TC bit), zone transfers and DNSSEC-sized answers

chapters.title: Resolution Workflow Step by Step
points: Cache check order: browser cache → OS cache/hosts file → recursive resolver cache; only a full miss triggers a walk down the hierarchy
Cold lookup of www.example.com: resolver asks root → gets referral to .com TLD NS → asks TLD → gets referral to example.com NS → asks authoritative → gets the A record
Recursive query: client says 'give me the final answer or an error' and the resolver does all the work (stub → resolver)
Iterative query: server replies with the best answer it has or a referral ('ask them'), and the asker follows it (resolver → root/TLD/authoritative)
Comparison: recursive = one request, resolver bears the load and caches; iterative = many requests, each server stays cheap; in practice a lookup uses both
Glue records: A/AAAA for a nameserver that lives inside the zone it serves (ns1.example.com for example.com) are supplied by the parent to avoid a circular lookup

chapters.title: Record Types That Matter
points: A maps a name to an IPv4 address; AAAA maps to an IPv6 address; a name can have multiple A/AAAA records (round-robin)
CNAME makes a name an alias of another name; it cannot coexist with other records at the same name, so it cannot sit at the zone apex (example.com) – use ALIAS/ANAME or A records there
MX gives mail servers with a priority number; lower value is tried first (10 mail1, 20 mail2); the target must be a hostname, not an IP, and not a CNAME
NS lists the authoritative nameservers for a zone and is what the parent uses to delegate; SOA holds the zone serial and timers
TXT holds free-form text, used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC and domain-ownership verification; PTR is the reverse IP → name record used for rDNS
Comparison table row: A→IPv4, AAAA→IPv6, CNAME→alias, MX→mail, NS→delegation, TXT→verification/policy

chapters.title: TTL and Caching
points: TTL is seconds a resolver may cache a record; it is set per record by the authoritative server and counts down in the resolver's cache
Low TTL (60–300 s) = faster change propagation but more queries; high TTL (3600–86400 s) = fewer queries but slow changes
Before a migration, lower the TTL at least one old-TTL ahead of the change, then switch the record, then raise TTL again
'DNS propagation' is really old cached answers expiring; there is no push, so you cannot force other resolvers to refresh
Negative caching: NXDOMAIN (name doesn't exist) is also cached, for the SOA minimum / negative TTL, so a just-created record can still look missing
Flush your own cache: ipconfig /flushdns (Windows), resolvectl flush-caches (systemd-resolved), sudo dscacheutil -flushcache (macOS)

chapters.title: dig and nslookup in Practice
points: dig example.com A +short prints just the answer; dig example.com MX / AAAA / TXT / NS queries other types
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com asks a specific resolver, handy to compare your resolver against a public one
dig +trace example.com does the iterative walk itself from the root, showing each referral – use it to find where delegation breaks
dig -x 203.0.113.5 does a reverse (PTR) lookup; read the ANSWER section, the TTL column and the status (NOERROR, NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL)
nslookup example.com, nslookup -type=MX example.com, nslookup example.com 8.8.8.8 mirror this; interactive mode with set type=; nslookup is older and less detailed than dig

Common mistakes: forgetting a trailing-dot FQDN in zone files, CNAME at the apex, MX pointing at a CNAME or IP, testing right after a change without checking TTL, editing the wrong zone because NS at the registrar differs from where you edited

chapters.title: DNS Cheat Sheet
points: Lookup flow: stub → recursive resolver (recursive query) → root → TLD → authoritative (iterative referrals) → answer cached for TTL
Records: A IPv4 · AAAA IPv6 · CNAME alias (not at apex) · MX mail with priority (lower wins) · NS delegation · TXT SPF/DKIM/verification · PTR reverse · SOA zone info
Status codes: NOERROR = ok, NXDOMAIN = name doesn't exist, SERVFAIL = server/DNSSEC failure, REFUSED = policy block
Debug commands: dig +short, dig @server, dig +trace, dig -x, nslookup -type=TYPE name server
Change safely: lower TTL first, wait the old TTL, change, verify with dig @authoritative, raise TTL
